title: Why Classroom Questioning Often Fails (and What to Do About It)
author: Christian Moore-Anderson
summary: Christian Moore-Anderson, drawing on chapter 5 of his book Difference Maker, diagnoses why open, single-concept classroom questions ('What is selection?', 'Why do plants transport water?') so often fail to generate participation. Grounding the argument in variation theory and Tsui's concept of 'common ground,' he argues that such questions leave students facing an unbounded, hidden space of possible correct aspects, producing a kind of mental paralysis in which the safest strategy is not to answer at all. Worse, teachers who encounter this silence often respond by narrowing subsequent questions to bare recall, unintentionally lowering the cognitive demand of the lesson. Moore-Anderson's proposed fix is to ask questions about differences rather than single concepts - a reformulation that establishes shared attention on a specific aspect and dramatically increases participation, illustrated by his own real-time correction of a farming question that initially drew blank faces. He closes with two easily-generated question templates - 'stability or change' and 'negative explanation' - that teachers of any subject can use to build variation directly into their questioning.
points: Moore-Anderson's core diagnosis: single-concept open questions ('What is a cell?') give students no indication of which aspect the teacher is targeting, producing a mental paralysis in which not participating feels like the safest bet.

His theoretical grounding: Tsui's concept of 'common ground' and variation theory explain why sharing focal awareness between teacher and student is a precondition for productive classroom questioning.

The unintended consequence he flags: when students stay silent on ambiguous questions, teachers often respond by narrowing future questions to simple recall, quietly lowering the cognitive demand of the lesson.

His practical fix: reformulate questions to ask about differences rather than single things - demonstrated by turning a blank-faced farming question into 'What difference would it make if a farmer populated a field using seeds, or cloned cuttings?', which immediately increased participation.

Two transferable question templates he offers for any subject: 'stability or change' (will X stay the same or change if Y happens?) and 'negative explanation' (why is this not like a plausible alternative?).
quotes: The expectation is unclear -- are they closed questions or open questions? All these questions are about single concepts, but with little indication to which aspect, and in relation to what.
So this is what the students think about. They puzzle over the possible aspects on their teacher's mind, instead of thinking deeply about the intended concept.

What likely occurs to many students in these questions is a sort of mental paralysis at the prospect of so many possible answers. They likely weigh the odds and assume their best bet is not to participate.
The key is to ask questions about differences, which clarify the aspect we're referring to. This will align expectations in the classroom.

I saw their blank faces and realised they had no idea what my expectation was. I then reformulated the question: "What difference would it make if a farmer populated a field using seeds, or cloned cuttings?" Participation increased immediately.
A requisite of good conversation is shared attention on the same aspect. To get that, ask questions about differences.
